lessons.title: Principles of Restoration: Accuracy and Authenticity
lessons.body:
Restoration means returning a building to a known earlier state by removing later additions or replacing missing elements. It is not renovation or remodelling. The two guiding principles are accuracy and authenticity. Accuracy means you base every decision on physical evidence, not guesswork. Authenticity means you use materials and techniques that match the original as closely as possible. In Africa, this often means working with local materials like laterite stone, coral rag, or mud brick, and using lime mortars instead of cement.

Start by asking: What is the earliest clear evidence of the building's form? That becomes your target. For example, if you find original window openings hidden behind a 1970s concrete block wall, you restore those openings to their original size and profile. If you cannot prove something existed, do not invent it. A common mistake is adding decorative elements that look old but were never there. That destroys authenticity.

Accuracy also applies to methods. If the original walls were built with mud mortar, using Portland cement will crack the old bricks because cement is harder and less breathable. Instead, mix lime putty with sand at a 1:3 ratio by volume. For coral stone walls in coastal Kenya or Tanzania, use a lime-based render with local sand and crushed coral. Test a small patch first: apply a 300mm x 300mm sample, let it cure for 7 days, then check for adhesion and colour match.

Authenticity is not about freezing a building in time. It is about honest repair. If a timber beam is rotten, replace only the rotten section with matching speciesâlike mvule or irokoâusing scarf joints. Do not cover it with epoxy that looks plastic. Keep a restoration log: date, location, material, and method. This log proves your work is accurate and helps future caretakers.

Finally, remember that restoration is reversible where possible. Use lime mortars and mechanical fixings that can be undone without damaging original fabric. Avoid strong adhesives or irreversible chemical treatments. The goal is to pass the building on to the next generation with its story intact, not to make it look new.

lessons.title: Documentation and Research for Restoration
lessons.body:
Before you touch a single stone, document everything. Restoration without documentation is destruction. You need three types of records: measured drawings, photographs, and written notes. Start with a simple sketch plan of each floor, then measure every room, door, window, and architectural feature. Use a 5-metre tape and a laser distance meter if available. Record dimensions in millimetres. For a typical 3-bedroom historic house, this takes 2-3 days.

Photograph every wall, ceiling, and floor before any work. Use a smartphone with good light. Take wide shots and close-ups of cracks, mouldings, and joints. Include a scaleâa ruler or a coinâin close-ups. Label each photo with room name and date. Store them in folders on a laptop or cloud drive. If you find old photos of the building in family albums or national archives, scan them at 300 dpi. These are gold for accuracy.

Research the building's history. Visit the local lands office to get the original title deed and any building plans. In many African cities, colonial-era plans are kept at national archivesâfor example, the Kenya National Archives in Nairobi or the National Archives of Ghana in Accra. Look for original specifications: brick sizes, timber species, roof pitch, and paint colours. Talk to elderly neighbours who remember the building before modifications. Record their stories with permission.

Material analysis helps. Take small samples of original mortar, plaster, and paint to a local university or laboratory. A simple acid test can tell you if mortar is lime-based (fizzes) or cement-based (does not fizz). For paint, a cross-section under a low-power microscope reveals layers. This costs about 500-1000 KES per sample but saves expensive mistakes.

Create a condition report. For each elementâwalls, roof, windows, doors, floorsânote its condition as good, fair, poor, or ruinous. Note what is original and what is later addition. Use a simple 1-5 scale. This report becomes your work plan. Without it, you will waste time and money restoring the wrong things. Keep a copy on site and one off site.

lessons.title: Restoring Architectural Features: Cornices and Moldings
lessons.body:
Cornices and moldings are the decorative bands that run along walls, ceilings, and openings. They are often the first things lost to neglect or bad repairs. Restoring them requires patience and a few simple tools: a profile gauge, a plasterer's float, a running mold, and a small trowel. In Africa, you can make a running mold from a piece of hardwood cut to the reverse profile of the molding.

First, clean the existing molding. Remove loose paint with a wire brush and scraper. Do not use a sanderâit rounds off sharp edges. If the molding is wood, check for rot with a screwdriver. Soft spots mean rot. Cut out rotten sections with a chisel and replace with matching timber. For plaster moldings, remove all loose material back to sound plaster. Wet the area with water before applying new plaster.

To replicate a missing section, use a profile gauge. Press the gauge against an intact part of the molding to copy its shape. Transfer that shape to a thin piece of zinc or hardwood. Cut it out with a coping saw and file smooth. This is your template. For simple cornices, you can build up layers with a plaster mix of 1 part lime putty to 2 parts fine sand. Apply with a small trowel, then run the template along a straight edge to form the profile. Work in 300mm sections. Let each section set for 30 minutes before moving on.

For large cornices, use a running mold. Fix a straight edge (a long spirit level or timber batten) to the wall. Mix plaster to a stiff consistency. Pack it into the corner, then pull the mold along the straight edge with a steady, even pressure. You may need two people: one to hold the straight edge, one to pull. Fill any gaps with a small trowel and smooth with a damp sponge.

After the plaster sets (24 hours), paint with a breathable lime wash or mineral paint. Do not use acrylic or vinyl paintâit traps moisture and causes the plaster to fail. For exterior cornices, add a water-repellent lime wash. Test a small area first. With practice, you can restore 2-3 metres of molding per day.

lessons.title: Replication of Historic Materials
lessons.body:
Historic buildings were built with local materials: mud brick, laterite, coral stone, limestone, timber, and lime. Replicating these materials is key to authentic restoration. Do not substitute modern materials just because they are cheaper or easier. They often cause damage. For example, cement render on a mud-brick wall traps moisture, leading to decay. Instead, use the same material or a compatible one.

Lime mortar is the most common historic binder. You can make it from lime putty (calcium hydroxide) and sand. In Africa, lime is available from suppliers in Kenya, South Africa, and Egypt. Mix 1 part lime putty to 3 parts sand by volume. Add water until it is workable. For a stronger mix, use 1:2. Let it cure slowlyâkeep it damp for 7 days. Lime mortar is breathable and flexible, so it moves with the building.

Mud brick (adobe) is common in West and East Africa. To replicate, dig clay soil, mix with straw or sisal fibres (about 10% by volume), and add water. Form bricks in wooden moulds and sun-dry for 2-3 weeks. Test the soil: roll a ball, let it dry, and see if it cracks. If it cracks too much, add sand. If it crumbles, add clay. For restoration, match the original brick sizeâoften 300mm x 150mm x 100mm.

Coral stone is used in coastal areas like Lamu, Zanzibar, and Mombasa. It is soft and porous. To replicate, source coral blocks from licensed quarries. Cut them with a hand saw or angle grinder with a diamond blade. Use lime mortar for bedding and pointing. Never use cementâit is too hard and will crack the coral.

Timber: Identify the original species. Common ones are mvule, iroko, mahogany, and teak. Source from sustainable local suppliers. For structural beams, use air-dried timber with less than 20% moisture content. For joinery, use quarter-sawn boards for stability. Treat with linseed oil or a borate solution for insectsânot creosote, which is toxic and banned in many countries.

Roofing: Historic roofs were often thatch, clay tiles, or corrugated iron. For thatch, use local grass or reeds, laid at a 45-degree pitch. For clay tiles, find a local potter to make copies. For corrugated iron, match the profile and gauge. Always use galvanised nails or copper nails to avoid rust stains.

lessons.title: Case Study: Restoring a Victorian Townhouse
lessons.body:
This case study is based on a real project in Cape Town, South Africa: a three-storey Victorian townhouse built in 1890. It had been converted into four flats in the 1960s, with dropped ceilings, concrete floors, and aluminium windows. The goal was to restore it to a single-family home while keeping original features.

Documentation: The team spent two weeks measuring and photographing. They found original plans at the Cape Town Deeds Office. The plans showed a central staircase, pressed metal ceilings, and sash windows. They also found a 1900 photograph in the local library. Total documentation cost: R15,000.

Removing later additions: They removed the dropped ceilings, revealing original pressed metal ceilings in three rooms. The metal was rusty but intact. They cleaned it with a wire brush, treated rust with phosphoric acid, and repainted with a zinc-rich primer and oil-based topcoat. They removed concrete floors to expose original yellowwood floorboards, which they sanded and sealed with linseed oil.

Restoring windows: The original sash windows had been replaced with aluminium. The team sourced matching Victorian sash windows from a demolition yard. They repaired rotten sills with epoxy wood filler (only for small areas) and replaced larger sections with meranti timber. They reglazed with 4mm glass and installed brass sash lifts. Cost per window: R2,500.

Cornices and moldings: The original cornices were damaged. They used a profile gauge to copy a surviving section, then made a running mold from hardwood. They mixed lime putty and fine sand (1:2) and ran new cornices in the main rooms. They also restored ceiling roses by casting new ones from plaster of Paris in silicone molds made from an intact original.

Modern code compliance: The building had to meet current fire and electrical codes. They installed a hidden sprinkler system in the ceiling void, upgraded wiring with conduit run behind skirting boards, and added a discreet fire escape at the rear. They insulated the roof with breathable wood fibre boards, not plastic foam.

Lessons learned: Budget 20% extra for surprises. Work with a structural engineer early. Keep a detailed log. The project took 14 months and cost R1.2 million. The restored townhouse now serves as a guesthouse, proving that heritage and income can coexist.

lessons.title: Balancing Restoration with Modern Building Codes
lessons.body:
Modern building codes exist for safety: fire, structural, electrical, and accessibility. Historic buildings often fail these codes because they were built before the codes existed. The challenge is to meet safety standards without destroying historic fabric. The solution is to integrate modern systems invisibly and use performance-based alternatives.

Fire safety: Most historic buildings have open staircases and no fire doors. You can add a fire suppression systemâlike a misting system using small-diameter pipesâthat runs behind cornices and under floors. For a 200mÂ² building, a mist system costs about $8,000-$12,000. It uses less water than sprinklers and causes less damage. Also, add intumescent paint to timber stairs and doors. This paint expands in a fire to insulate the wood, giving 30-60 minutes of fire resistance. It can be painted over to match original colours.

Structural: Old buildings often have inadequate foundations or rotten lintels. Instead of replacing entire walls, use helical ties and resin anchors to stitch cracks. For sagging floors, add steel beams below the joists, but conceal them in the ceiling void. Work with a structural engineer who has heritage experience. In South Africa, the National Heritage Resources Act requires a permit for any alteration to a building older than 60 years.

Electrical: Rewiring is usually necessary. Run new cables in existing voidsâbehind skirting boards, under floorboards, and in ceiling spaces. Use conduit where exposed. Install modern circuit breakers and earth leakage. For lighting, use LED bulbs that mimic the colour of original incandescent (2700K). Avoid surface-mounted trunking on historic walls.

Accessibility: Ramps and lifts are hard to add without impact. For a small building, a platform lift can be installed in a discreet location, like a former coal store. For steps, add a removable timber ramp that matches the floor finish. For toilets, convert a later addition rather than a historic room.

Plumbing: Use copper or PEX pipes, but run them in existing service ducts. For bathrooms, avoid moving original walls. Use a raised floor system to hide pipes, or run them in the ceiling void of the room below.

Document everything you add. Keep a log of all modern interventions. Use reversible fixingsâscrews, not nails or glue. The goal is to make the building safe for today while preserving its ability to tell its story tomorrow. Always get approvals from local heritage authorities before starting work.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Restoration Principles, Materials & Compliance for African Built Heritage

Restoration is the most technically demandingâand commercially rewardingâintervention in the preservation toolkit. For African contractors, conservation architects, and heritage developers, it is also a business discipline: every decision on mortar mix, moulding profile, or code compliance carries cost, risk, and reputational consequence. This Practical Reference consolidates the core principles from the module into an operational guide for professionals working on historic buildings across the continent, from the Victorian-era merchant houses of Lagos and Cape Town to the Swahili stone towns of Lamu and Zanzibar, and the colonial-era administrative buildings of Nairobi and Accra.

Why Restoration Is a Business Proposition in Africa

Africa's heritage building stock is under-monetised. A restored building commands premium rents in heritage tourism corridors, qualifies for cultural heritage incentives in several jurisdictions, and can anchor mixed-use districts where new-builds cannot obtain planning consent. The 2023 African World Heritage Fund reported that less than 15% of listed heritage properties on the continent generate revenue sufficient to fund their own maintenanceâmeaning restoration is not merely a conservation activity but an investment requiring a defensible return. Restoration projects that fail commercially usually fail for three reasons: inaccurate documentation leading to rework, inappropriate materials causing accelerated decay, and late code-compliance conflicts forcing redesign. This reference addresses all three.

Principles of Restoration: Accuracy and Authenticity

Accuracy means the work matches the historic fabric in form, dimension, and performance. Authenticity means it matches in material, technique, and provenance. The two are not interchangeable. A cornice can be dimensionally accurate (correct profile) but inauthentic (cast in modern epoxy rather than lime plaster). For African projects, authenticity is complicated by material sourcing: historic lime was often produced from local limestone or coral rag, and modern bagged lime may differ in hydraulic set and porosity. The rule for practitioners: match the substrate's vapour permeability and thermal expansion before matching colour or finish. Where original materials are unavailable, document the substitution explicitly in the conservation record.

Documentation and Research

No restoration should begin without a measured survey, a condition assessment, and a documentary history. Minimum deliverables for a fundable project: (1) measured drawings at 1:50 and 1:20 for detail areas; (2) photographic condition survey with date stamps; (3) materials analysisâmortar, plaster, paint stratigraphy; (4) archival research including land records, historic photographs, and where possible oral histories. In many African jurisdictions, national museums and heritage councils hold archival material, but access may require formal application. Budget 3â8% of project cost for documentation; this is the cheapest insurance against rework.

Restoring Architectural Features: Cornices and Moldings

Cornices, moldings, and decorative plasterwork are the highest-visibility elements of a restoration and the most common source of client dissatisfaction. The technical sequence is: (1) record surviving profiles by template or photogrammetry; (2) identify substrate and original mix; (3) remove only failed materialânever strip sound historic plaster; (4) build up in thin coats, allowing full carbonation between coats; (5) finish to match surface texture, not just profile. In humid coastal contexts such as Mombasa or Dar es Salaam, specify a final limewash or breathable mineral paint; acrylic paints trap moisture and cause salt crystallisation behind the finish.

Replication of Historic Materials

Material replication is where African projects most often go wrong. Modern cement mortar is harder, less permeable, and thermally incompatible with historic brick, stone, and coral rag. The result is spalling within 5â10 years. Table 1 summarises compatible substitutions tested in African conditions.

Table 1. Historic material replication guide for African contexts (selected).
Historic material Common modern substitute Recommended restoration approach Key risk if mismatched
Lime mortar (non-hydraulic) OPC cement mortar NHL 2 or 3.5, or air lime putty with local sand; match aggregate grading Spalling of masonry; trapped moisture
Coral rag stone Concrete block New coral rag from licensed quarry; lime mortar bedding Differential movement; loss of authenticity
Clay brick (handmade) Machine brick Salvaged or bespoke handmade brick; lime mortar Differential expansion; cracking
Lime plaster Gypsum or cement render Lime putty with hair or fibre; three-coat build-up Trapped salts; surface failure
Timber (local hardwood) Treated softwood or imported hardwood Species-matched timber; borate treatment; breathable finish Movement, rot, termite vulnerability
Wrought iron Mild steel Wrought-iron replacement or galvanised steel with isolation Galvanic corrosion at fixings

Sources: ICOMOS (2003) Charter â Principles for the Analysis, Conservation and Structural Restoration of Architectural Heritage; ICCROM/UNESCO (2016) Preserving African Cultural Heritage; and field guidance from the African World Heritage Fund (2023).

Case Study: Restoring a Victorian Townhouse

Consider a two-storey Victorian townhouse in a coastal African cityâthe type found in Lagos (Brazilian Quarter), Cape Town (Bo-Kaap fringe), or Freetown. Typical defects: cement render over original lime plaster, corroded iron balconies, failed timber sash windows, and a leaking roof. A commercially viable restoration sequence is: emergency weatherproofing first (roof, gutters, downpipes), then structural stabilisation, then envelope repair, then services, then finishes. The mistake most contractors make is starting with finishes because they are visible to the client. This inverts the risk profile: finishes applied before the envelope is dry will fail within one rainy season.

Cost benchmarks for a 250 mÂ² townhouse in an African heritage context typically fall between USD 180,000 and USD 420,000 for full restoration, depending on structural condition and extent of replication. The premium over equivalent new-build is 25â60%, but restored heritage properties in tourism-active locations can achieve rental yields 1.5â2.5 times comparable new-build stock. The business case is strongest when restoration is paired with adaptive reuseâboutique accommodation, gallery, or mixed-use retailârather than pure residential.

Balancing Restoration with Modern Building Codes

African building codes are generally written for new construction and rarely contain heritage-specific provisions. The practical approach is a performance-based equivalence argument: demonstrate that the restored building achieves the same life-safety outcome (structural, fire, egress) as a code-compliant new building, even if the method differs. Table 2 sets out the common conflict points and tested workarounds.

Table 2. Common code conflicts in heritage restoration and practical resolutions.
Code requirement Conflict with historic fabric Performance-based resolution Documentation needed
Fire resistance of structural elements Original timber floors and stairs Intumescent coatings, sprinkler compensation, or fire-rated lining concealed Fire engineer's report; heritage authority approval
Minimum egress width Narrow historic staircases Alternative egress route; upgraded lighting; reduced occupancy load Egress analysis; occupancy calculation
Thermal performance (energy) Single-glazed sash windows; solid walls Secondary glazing; internal insulation with breathable membrane; draught-proofing Energy model; condensation risk assessment
Accessibility (ramps, lifts) Historic entrance steps; narrow doorways Discreet platform lift; reversible ramp; alternative accessible entrance Access consultant report; reversibility statement
Structural loading (imposed) Timber floor capacity Local strengthening; load limitation; new independent structure Structural engineer's calculations
Damp-proof course Solid walls, no DPC Breathable remedial treatments; improved drainage; ventilation Damp survey; materials specification

Sources: ICOMOS (2003); UNESCO/ICCROM (2016); and comparative review of national building codes in Kenya, South Africa, Nigeria, and Ghana (2020â2024).

â  SAFETY WARNING â LEAD PAINT AND ASBESTOS IN HISTORIC FABRIC

Buildings constructed or refurbished before the 1980s may contain lead-based paint, asbestos cement sheeting, asbestos pipe lagging, or asbestos-backed floor tiles. In many African jurisdictions, asbestos is still present in heritage building stock and enforcement of removal regulations is inconsistent. Do not sand, scrape, or demolish suspect materials without a licensed asbestos survey and, where lead paint is present, without lead-safe work practices. Exposure causes irreversible health harm and exposes the contractor to legal liability. Budget for specialist removal and disposal at a licensed facility before any restoration work begins in affected areas. This is a non-negotiable pre-construction cost, not a contingency item.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Document before you touch. Measured survey, photographic condition record, and materials analysis completed and filed before any intervention.
  2. Match permeability, not appearance. Specify lime-based mortars, plasters, and breathable finishes where historic fabric is lime-based or porous.
  3. Weatherproof first. Roof, gutters, drainage, and damp control before any internal or decorative work.
  4. Preserve sound historic fabric. Remove only what is failed; retain and repair wherever structurally feasible.
  5. Reversibility. New interventions should be removable without damage to historic fabricâdocument the method.
  6. Code strategy early. Engage fire, structural, and access engineers at concept stage, not after design freeze.
  7. Hazard survey before work. Asbestos and lead paint surveys completed and remediated before restoration commences.
  8. Conservation record at handover. Photographic and written record of all interventions, materials, and approvals delivered to the client and heritage authority.

Further Reading

  • ICOMOS â Charters and Texts (free access to the 2003 Charter and related doctrine)
  • UNESCO World Heritage Centre â Capacity Building and Heritage Conservation Resources
  • ICCROM â Free conservation resources and technical guidance
  • African World Heritage Fund â Reports and project guidance for African heritage sites
  • Getty Conservation Institute â Free technical publications on materials and restoration practice

This Practical Reference is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills course Buildings for Preservation (10 Methods), Module: Method 3 â Restoration. Prepared for professional use in African heritage contexts. Verify all material specifications and code interpretations with the relevant national heritage authority and building control office before implementation.

quiz.q: What are the two guiding principles of restoration?
quiz.explanation: Restoration must be based on evidence (accuracy) and use original materials and techniques (authenticity).

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using Portland cement on historic mud-brick walls?
options: B) It is not available in Africa
C) It is harder and less breathable, causing cracks
quiz.explanation: Cement is harder than mud brick and traps moisture, leading to decay and cracking.

quiz.q: What is a simple test to determine if a mortar is lime-based?
options: B) Add acid and look for fizzing
D) Scratch it with a fingernail
quiz.explanation: Lime mortar reacts with acid and fizzes, while cement mortar does not.

quiz.q: How long should you keep a lime mortar patch damp during curing?
quiz.explanation: Lime mortar needs to cure slowly and stay damp for about 7 days to gain strength.

quiz.q: What tool is used to copy the profile of an existing molding?
quiz.explanation: A profile gauge has movable pins that copy the shape of a molding.

quiz.q: What is the correct mix ratio for lime putty to sand for general restoration mortar?
quiz.explanation: A 1:3 mix of lime putty to sand is standard for breathable, flexible mortar.

quiz.q: Which material should never be used to point coral stone walls?
quiz.explanation: Cement is too hard and will crack the soft coral stone.

quiz.q: What is the first step in any restoration project?
quiz.explanation: Documentation provides the evidence needed for accurate restoration decisions.

quiz.q: How many days does it typically take to measure and photograph a 3-bedroom historic house?
quiz.explanation: Thorough documentation of a small house takes about 2-3 days.

quiz.q: Where can you often find original building plans in African countries?
quiz.explanation: National archives, like the Kenya National Archives, hold colonial-era building plans.

quiz.q: What is a running mold used for?
quiz.explanation: A running mold is pulled along a straight edge to create continuous moldings.

quiz.q: What is the correct consistency for plaster when using a running mold?
quiz.explanation: Stiff plaster holds its shape when the mold is pulled.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid acrylic paint on restored lime plaster?
options: B) It traps moisture and causes failure
quiz.explanation: Acrylic paint is not breathable and traps moisture, leading to plaster decay.

quiz.q: What is the typical curing time for a new plaster molding before painting?
quiz.explanation: Plaster needs at least 24 hours to set before painting.

quiz.q: Which timber species is commonly used for restoration in East Africa?
quiz.explanation: Mvule is a durable local hardwood often found in historic buildings.

quiz.q: What percentage of straw or fibre is typically added to mud bricks?
quiz.explanation: About 10% straw or sisal fibre by volume improves tensile strength.

quiz.q: How long should sun-dried mud bricks cure before use?
quiz.explanation: Mud bricks need 2-3 weeks of sun-drying to gain strength.

quiz.q: What is the best treatment for historic timber to protect against insects?
quiz.explanation: Linseed oil or borate solutions are safe and effective, unlike toxic creosote.

quiz.q: In the Victorian townhouse case study, what was found under the dropped ceilings?
quiz.explanation: The dropped ceilings concealed original pressed metal ceilings.

quiz.q: How much extra budget should you plan for surprises in restoration?
quiz.explanation: A 20% contingency is recommended for unexpected discoveries.

quiz.q: What type of fire suppression system is least damaging to historic fabric?
quiz.explanation: Misting systems use less water and can be hidden in voids.

quiz.q: What does intumescent paint do?
options: B) Expands in fire to insulate wood
quiz.explanation: Intumescent paint expands when heated, providing fire resistance to timber.

quiz.q: How can you hide new electrical cables in a historic building?
options: B) Run in existing voids behind skirting
quiz.explanation: Running cables in existing voids keeps them invisible and preserves historic walls.

quiz.q: What colour temperature LED bulbs mimic original incandescent lighting?
quiz.explanation: 2700K LEDs give a warm light similar to old incandescent bulbs.

quiz.q: What is a reversible fixing?
quiz.explanation: Screws can be removed without damaging original fabric, unlike nails or glue.

quiz.q: In South Africa, what act requires a permit for altering buildings older than 60 years?
quiz.explanation: The National Heritage Resources Act protects heritage buildings and requires permits.

quiz.q: What is the first step when replicating a missing cornice?
options: B) Copy a surviving profile with a gauge
quiz.explanation: You need an accurate template from an existing section to replicate the profile.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep a restoration log?
options: B) To prove accuracy and help future caretakers
quiz.explanation: A log documents decisions and methods, ensuring authenticity and guiding future work.

quiz.q: What is the recommended pitch for a thatched roof?
quiz.explanation: A 45-degree pitch is typical for effective thatch drainage.

quiz.q: What type of nails should be used for corrugated iron roofing to avoid rust stains?
quiz.explanation: Galvanised or copper nails resist rust and prevent staining.
